# Naming conventions

## Semantic:
- Apply the rule of 'compound nouns' to every name (of any type) created.
- The `ops` tools are defined as tools from the fields of `DevOps`, `SecOps` and `CloudOps` (the list may be extended).
- Follow the name-building scheme `objectClassifierObjectClassifier`, where `object` is synonymous with 'noun' and `classifier` is synonymous with 'adjective'. The first 'object' in the chain is called the `primary word` for the purposes of this notation. The exact case of the `objectClassifierObjectClassifier` scheme depends on the context of programming language, or existing guidelines. It is universally applied to all cases.
- This scheme must remain compatible with the naming conventions of the programming language of the file being worked on.
- Every `function`, `method`, `lambda` (or functionally similar `code constructs`) must have its name suffixed with a '_verb' in its base (infinitive) form, where the `verb` defines its main functionality. Example: a function calculating the offset of coordinates must be named 'offset_coordinates_calculate'.
- The `primary word` (the first 'noun' of the compound-noun semantic chain) must refer to the most general 'class' (conceptual 'root') of the item. However, when the context defines multiple compound-noun words in a specific group, that group should be the `primary word` candidate. Example: a variable defining the length of a science book must be named 'length_book_science', as multiple other variables (within the group) will follow. Otherwise, if the context defines the class of 'book' that instead contains the length variables, the 'length' object is the last.
- When working with statically typed programming languages, the 'variable' (in the conceptual sense) should **not** carry a type annotation in its name. However, when the language is dynamically typed, the variable name must be suffixed with its exact type. This type must exactly match one of the built-in types of the programming language.
- When the programming language does not natively support static typing, yet this form of typing is officially supported using type annotations and guardrails, treat such a language as one of the natively statically typed programming languages. Example: Python.
- TERRAFORM: This rule partially applies to certain statically typed languages (such as HCL, in Terraform and its derivatives), where the suffix should only define the collection type of the object. An object with a one-dimensional index should be suffixed with '_list', '_set' or '_map', while objects with an index of two or more dimensions are suffixed with '_object'. The exact form of the suffixes should remain compatible with the guidelines of the language.
- TERRAFORM: When working with one of the `ops` tools, such as Terraform, the `primary word` is always the name of the `deployment` that the `object`, `variable`, `local`, `input`, `output` (and so on) belongs to. Example: a `local` value in Terraform defining a `list` of `Storage Account` names within the 'FrontEnd' deployment must be named 'frontend_st_list'.
- Entry-point functions follow the same scheme and are named after what the script does, as a script may also act as a module that carries out one function. Example: 'report_generate', not 'main'.
- Write every word of a name in full, without abbreviations (e.g. 'length', not 'len'; 'index', not 'i'). Only widely known abbreviations and acronyms stay (e.g. 'csv', 'url', 'id', 'md').
- Name a collection in the plural and each of its items in the singular. Example: 'for book in books'.
- When working with class-specific variables, the `primary word` is always the direct class name, preceded by its parent classes (in top-down order), if any exist. Example: a constant referencing the maximum height of the class `cat`, derived from the class `animals`, must be written as 'animals_cat_height'.
- Apply the same scheme to the names of files and generated artefacts (exports, renders, assets). Start with the most general component the file belongs to, follow it with the part, and end with the part's variant or kind, so that the files of one component sort together and can be found by their component alone.
- Keep the name of a generated file identical to the identifier that produces it (such as a parameter selecting the part to export), apart from a prefix shared by all files of the same source.

## Technical:
- This convention was authored by 'Mateusz Adamczyk'. It is derived from certain semantic rules of the Polish and German languages, and influenced by `Hungarian notation` and The Ohio State University's "File Naming Convention Best Practices" guide.
- This convention applies to programming languages and similar Turing-complete tools, as well as declarative configuration language families (such as HCL), and to the names of files and generated artefacts.
- Always prioritise language-specific guidelines where they exist, and apply this convention only as a non-conflicting extension of them.
